newsitem.title: UK: Mark hovers as market eyes Bundesbank meeting.
newsitem.headline: Mark hovers as market eyes Bundesbank meeting.

text.p: The mark was supported on its European crosses in morning trade as the market bet the Bundesbank would make a last effort to talk down the dollar after its final meeting before the summer recess.
"The key event for the market will be the Bundesbank meeting and their review of the money supply target," said Hans-Guenter Redeker, senior economist at Chase Investment Bank in London.
"We know that they are not happy with the current exchange rate level and especially not with the pace of the mark's decline...The market is betting on verbal intervention," he said.

The mark, which has sunk to multi-year lows against sterling and the dollar, has been torn to shreds by the perception that the launch of European monetary union will involve some of the EU's less strong economies and thus the euro will be soft.
The French 1997 budget projection released this week showed France did not expect to meet the deficit target of 3.0 percent of GDP laid down in the Maastricht Treaty.
On Tuesday, three senior Bundesbank officials said the treaty did not insist that the 3.0 percent ratio be met exactly but said sustainability of the deficit reductions was more important.

Traders said the acceptance of deviations from the 3.0 percent deficit target will make it more difficult for Germany to object to the inclusion of weaker currencies. Such concerns have hit the mark as the market contemplates its replacement with a softer euro.

French Finance Minister Dominique Strauss-Kahn's urging that Italy, Spain and Portugal be included in the first wave of EMU in an interview with German weekly Die Zeit intensified this sentiment. He said convergence was more important for EMU entry than hitting an exact target.
The doubts have pushed EMU safe-haven currencies like sterling, the Swiss franc and Swedish crown higher.

By 0945 GMT the mark was at 972.50/2.80 lire compared to 972.40/70 late Wednesday. Mark/Paris stood at 3.3712/17 versus 3.3706/11. Mark/swiss was at 81.15/25 compared to 81.28/38 and mark/Spain was at 84.23/4.26 compared to 84.22/4.24.
An economist at Daiwa Europe said the Bundesbank would not step in as tyhe mark was not at such an uncomfortable level.
"The Bundesbank will sit back and need further evidence before going in and intervening, and certainly before they consider moving monetary policy," the econoimist said.

The economist added some dealers expected a change in monetary policy, or a move from the fixed repo rate to a variable one, but referred to this sentiment as "rabid overreaction" to the mark's decline.
During the last two weeks the market has been bombarded with German statements to halt the mark's slide.
The latest came from German independent economic advisor or "wise man" Rolf Peffekoven this morning, saying he did not expect the dollar to continue its rapid advance against the mark.
He added that the Group of Seven leading industrial nations could interven to halt the dollar's rise.
So far traders have reacted little to the comments which have, at best, only served to provide a brief respite in the mark's fall.
Any verbal intervention today would not prove to affect the medium term downward trend of the mark as it was based on fundamentals, analysts said.
"It could drop two pfennigs (against the dollar) without changing the medium term trend in the market," Redeker said.
"It's very much backed up by fundamentals...The German economy doesn't look too healthy."
By 1000 GMT dollar/mark was at 1.8264/74 compared to late Wednesday's 1.8240/50.
Analysts pointed to a rise in corporation tax in Germany and France which would hamper the investment cycle leaving domestic demand and the labour market to suffer the consequences.
"Without any rise in investment activity you won't see a like improvement in the labour market...We could even get another wave of unemployment coming in Autumn-winter this year," Redeker said.
Michael Lewis, senior international economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell, said he did not expect the Bundesbank to intervene or change monetary policy despite the state of the mark.
"There's no obstacle to further mark weakness," he said.
-Nicholas Winning, London newsroom +44 171 542 6701
